claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, intrinsic hardness and strength are primarily governed by lattice distortion arising from atomic-size mismatch.
Randomly distributed elements with different atomic radii produce variations in interatomic distances and a severely distorted lattice in HEAs.
Lattice distortions impede dislocation motion by increasing local energy barriers.
Controlled casting or solidification can provide a homogeneous, disordered, equiatomic single-phase BCC or FCC HEA for the comparison.

Atomic-size mismatch can be varied while valence-electron concentration, processing history, and phase stability are held constant by replacing a constituent with an element having similar chemical behavior but a different atomic radius.
Below approximately 800 °C, the proposed samples will remain single-phase solid solutions in which dislocation glide governs deformation.
The degree of lattice distortion can be represented by the spread in interatomic distances.
XRD peak broadening or pair-distribution-function analysis can quantify the relevant degree of lattice distortion.
Greater atomic-size disparity produces stronger lattice distortion.
The distorted lattice pins dislocations, raises activation barriers for slip, and reduces dislocation mobility.
Lattice distortion contributes to elevated hardness and strength in HEAs.
Otherwise similar single-phase HEAs with greater lattice distortion will have statistically higher hardness and tensile yield strength than alloys with less distortion.
The higher-distortion alloys will retain ductility analogous to that of the lower-distortion controls.
A control HEA with minimal atomic-size variance will have a more uniform lattice and lower resistance to dislocation motion.
Lattice-distortion strengthening should dominate in well-homogenized, single-phase HEAs when precipitation and ordering effects are minimal.
At very high temperatures, or after multiphase or recrystallized microstructures form, other mechanisms may obscure the lattice-distortion effect.
The quantitative relationship between atomic-size mismatch and strengthening, including interactions with precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening, remains undetermined.

Failure to observe a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase in the verified higher-distortion series, or observation of a reversed trend, would falsify lattice distortion as the primary mediator under the controlled conditions.
